claims.text: Superconducting behavior in high-entropy alloys is governed by the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
Chemical disorder modulates the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
Atomic-scale lattice distortions modulate the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
The initial high-entropy alloy has a random distribution of constituent elements.
The initial alloy contains no pre-existing superconducting phase.
Changing the relative concentrations of constituent elements produces controlled variations in chemical disorder.
Chemical disorder and lattice distortions affect the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
The electronic density of states at the Fermi level influences electron-phonon coupling strength.
Electron-phonon coupling strength is critical for superconductivity in the proposed HEAs.
The superconducting transition temperature will vary systematically with chemical disorder.
Changes in superconducting transition temperature will correlate with changes in the density of states at the Fermi level.
The proposed governing mechanism applies to metallic-bonded HEAs.
The proposed governing mechanism does not apply to HEAs with dominant covalent or ionic bonding.
Low-temperature resistivity can be used to determine the superconducting transition temperature.
Photoemission spectroscopy can measure the electronic density of states at the Fermi level in the proposed samples.
Failure of Tc to correlate with the Fermi-level density of states would falsify the hypothesis.
